# HOW WE FUND THE NEXT DOUBLING
## A staged capital stack: price first, secured debt second, minority equity only for the money we cannot get back

**Board decision paper | v1.0**
*(Term-sheet drafts, lender term-sheet comparisons and the Gate 0 research brief sit in Annex 1–3 and are not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of (i) the **control floor** in §2 as a binding rule against which every instrument is tested; (ii) the **sequencing principle** in §5 — price, then working-capital debt, then asset-backed capex debt, then equity for irrecoverable spend; (iii) the **funding structure and drawdown order** in §6, with a total committed envelope of €[32]m of which €[14]m is equity; (iv) the **staging gates** in §7 and the **walk-away red lines** in §8; and (v) **€220k (plus €40k contingency) to fund Gate 0**, a six-week verification programme. No instrument is signed and no valuation is accepted at this meeting. The equity price decision becomes irrevocable only at Gate 3.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

We are not short of capital in aggregate; we are short of it for about **[20] months**. Base-case cumulative funding gap peaks at €[20]m in month [22] and self-liquidates from FY3 as the capacity we are buying converts to cash — so the correct answer is a **timing structure, not a single raise** (§3.3). We recommend, in this order: **(1) a realised price increase of [4]%** on the constrained order book, which is the cheapest capital available to us — non-dilutive, covenant-free, immediately effective, and it rations scarce capacity toward better customers (§4.1); **(2) customer deposits and capacity-reservation prepayments** of €[4]m against long-lead orders; **(3) a €[10]m borrowing-base revolver** secured on receivables and inventory only, funding working-capital build; **(4) €[14]m of equipment finance** secured on the machines it buys, no all-asset debenture and no personal guarantees; and **(5) €[14]m of minority primary equity in two tranches (€8m + €6m)**, the second at a pre-agreed step-up, used **only** for the irrecoverable spend — hiring, market entry, brand, systems — because that spend has no collateral value and must not be financed with instruments that can foreclose. We reject the framing that this is a valuation dispute: on the arithmetic in §4.4, the difference between the fund's €[110]m and the founders' €[150]m is worth ~[2] points of founder ownership, while a single bad structural term (2× participating preference plus accruing dividend) is worth ~[19]m of founder proceeds at a €[200]m exit. **Price is the small variable; terms are the large one.** We also reject the assumption that debt protects control: a maintenance-covenant bank facility hands a credit committee an effective veto over capex, hiring and acquisitions, and in the stress case in §9 it is the only instrument in this paper that can cost us the company. Two claims here are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that demand genuinely exceeds capacity at a *higher* price, and that the competitive window is [18–30] months rather than [6]. Gate 0 tests exactly those two, and §7.4 states in advance what result flips the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Security law, tax treatment of interest/warrants, statutory consent thresholds, our own audited accounts | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and auditors |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Current market terms for growth debt and minority equity, capex quotes, customer re-qualification cycles, price elasticity | Lender/investor market terms ±[150]bps and structurally variable. **Competitive-window duration: ±[50]% at best** | Gate 0, by CFO + adviser + customer interviews |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our leverage cap, dilution floor, growth rate, tranche sizes, price increase | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1–3, by this Board |

A number in this paper that is not tagged has not been thought through. **Market norms for terms are [R], not [V]** — nothing in §8 should be treated as "standard" until a term sheet is in front of counsel.

### 0.2 Declared baseline (to be confirmed at Gate 0)

| Item | Figure | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| FY0 revenue | €[60]m | [V] |
| Growth rate achieved | ~[41]% CAGR (doubling every [24] months) | [V] |
| Gross margin | [46]% | [V] |
| EBITDA / margin | €[8.4]m / [14]% | [V] |
| EBITDA→operating cash conversion | [55]% (working-capital build absorbs the rest) | [V] |
| Working capital intensity | [22]% of revenue | [V] |
| Net debt / undrawn facilities | €[4]m / €[3]m | [V] |
| Ownership | Founders [78]%, angels [14]%, ESOP [8]% | [V] |
| Current capacity ceiling | ships €[75]m/yr at full utilisation | [R] |
| Qualified demand / pipeline | €[105]m/yr equivalent | [R] |
| Capex intensity of new capacity | €[0.24] per €1 of annual revenue capacity | [R] |
| Plan: FY1 / FY2 / FY3 revenue | €[84]m / €[118]m / €[160]m | [D] |
| Post-tax incremental ROIC on capacity spend | **[28]%** (§3.4) | [R] |

### 0.3 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| Funding the capacity, hiring and market-entry plan to FY3 | Sale of the company; majority recapitalisation |
| Instrument choice, sequencing, staging and red lines | Choice of which new geographies to enter (separate paper) |
| Control architecture (board, reserved matters, exit rights) | Founder estate planning and personal tax |
| Partial founder secondary as a risk-management tool | Any transaction taking founders below the §2 control floor |
| Pricing as a financing instrument | Full pricing-strategy overhaul beyond the constrained book |

### 0.4 The rule of this document

**Every financing option carries a stated cost to the core business**, not only a cost of capital. Diligence consumes the CEO and CFO; covenants consume the finance function monthly; investor boards consume preparation days. These are quantified in §10 and are part of the comparison in §3.5, not a footnote to it.

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Debt or equity? | Which *slice* of the requirement are we funding — recoverable assets, self-liquidating working capital, or unrecoverable expansion opex — and what is the correct instrument for that slice? (§3.3) |
| Is the growth fund's valuation fair? | What is the **total structural cost** of their offer — preference, participation, dividend, ratchet, redemption, drag, board — expressed in euros of founder proceeds at three exit values? (§4.4) |
| How do we keep control? | Control is board seats, reserved matters and forced-exit rights, not percentage. Which instrument gives away the most *decision rights* per euro raised? (§2) |

**Corollary 1 — the cheapest capital is a price increase.** If demand exceeds capacity at current prices, our price is below clearing. A [4]% realised increase on the constrained book adds ~€[2.4]m of annual EBITDA **[D]**, is instantly available, dilutes nobody, and reduces the amount of external capital required by roughly €[7]m over the plan. Any financing paper that starts with instruments has skipped its first option.

**Corollary 2 — debt can cost more control than equity.** A minority round at €[110]m pre takes founders from [78]% to ~[69]% and, if structured to the §2 floor, changes no operating decision. A €[24]m all-asset senior facility with a [2.5]× maintenance leverage covenant gives a credit committee a de facto veto on capex, hiring and acquisitions in every quarter where headroom is thin — and in the §9 stress case, the power to enforce. **Dilution is a price; covenant breach is a transfer of the company.**

---

## §2 The control floor (a rule, not a preference)

Founders hold [78]%, comfortably above the [50]% ordinary-resolution and [75]% special-resolution thresholds **[V — confirm for our jurisdiction]**. Percentage is therefore *not* the binding constraint today; decision rights are. The following are binding on management in every negotiation. Any instrument that cannot be structured within them is declined, irrespective of price.

| # | Floor | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Founder economic ownership | never below **[55]%** pre-exit **[D]** |
| F2 | Board |

# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v2.0**
*(The management committee counterpart, with vendor-level detail and the full research brief, is Annex 1 and is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is the main way strategy papers mislead their own authors.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and a customs broker |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade and customs data: ±[15]%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±[40]% at best** | Gate 0, by field research |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this Board |

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk rather than merely noting it.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU law regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | Category extension beyond market-fit adaptation |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is not a slogan; it is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw). A line item in this paper without a named cost to the core has not been thought through.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: revenue €[78]m **[R]**, gross margin [58]%, EBITDA [8.5]%, [210] FTE, [62]% of revenue in DE/NL/Nordics, wholesale/DTC split [55/45].

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

**Corollary 1 — cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in landed cost. A [15]% FOB saving **[D]** is erased by an [11.5]% MFN duty if origin fails **[V]**, by a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, by a [2]-point defect rate, or by one labour finding that costs a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are landed-cost-after-risk decisions.



[NEW REQUEST]
A profitable scale-up doubling revenue every two years has an opportunity to accelerate: demand exceeds capacity, and a rival is raising heavily to chase the same market. The founders hold 78% equity and prize independence; the company generates cash but not enough to fund the required capacity, hiring, and market expansion simultaneously. Banks offer covenant-heavy debt, growth funds offer capital at a valuation the founders consider low, and going slower risks ceding the market window.

Recommend a growth-financing strategy. Compare debt, minority equity, hybrid instruments, and disciplined organic growth against the company's risk tolerance, the competitive window, and the founders' control preferences; propose a funding structure, the milestones it should be staged against, and the walk-away conditions for each source.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

[END PREVIOUS OUTPUT]

# Critic Review — "Growth-Financing Strategy" request

## 1. Blocking finding: there is no output to review

The `[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]` block is empty. Nothing was produced against the new request. This is a hard fail regardless of any other consideration, and it cannot be scored on quality, only on absence.

The only substantive content in the packet is the *prior* deliverable — a v2.0 board paper on international demand/supply entry for a €78m apparel brand. That artefact answers a different question for what appears to be a different company (no mention of 78% founder equity, doubling revenue, capacity constraints, or a funded rival). A redraft must not silently inherit its facts.

Because there is nothing to critique line-by-line, the remainder of this review functions as a specification the next draft will be judged against, plus the failure modes most likely to appear in a first attempt.

## 2. What the request actually demands (a completeness checklist)

The prompt contains five explicit deliverables. A draft missing any one of them is incomplete:

1. **A recommended growth-financing strategy** (a single position, not a menu).
2. **A four-way comparison** — debt / minority equity / hybrid instruments / disciplined organic growth — **evaluated against three named criteria**: risk tolerance, competitive window, founders' control preferences. This is a 4×3 grid at minimum; prose that discusses each option in isolation without cross-comparison on the same axes does not satisfy it.
3. **A proposed funding structure** — instruments, amounts, order of drawdown, sources.
4. **Staging milestones** — what unlocks each tranche.
5. **Walk-away conditions for each source** — five sets (including organic), pre-committed and testable.

Two of these (4 and 5) are where generic strategy writing usually collapses into platitude. "Revisit if performance deteriorates" is not a walk-away condition. "Decline any term sheet with a >1x participating preference, a redemption right inside 7 years, or investor consent over hiring/budget below €Xm" is.

## 3. Errors of framing the redraft is likely to make

**(a) Treating this as a valuation dispute when it is a structure dispute.** The founders think the growth fund's price is low. The paper must test whether *price* or *terms* is the binding constraint. A "low" headline valuation with a clean 1x non-participating preference, no ratchet, and a founder-majority board may be cheaper than a high headline number carrying a 2x participating preference and a redemption put. Any draft that argues about pre-money multiples without decomposing structural cost has missed the actual decision.

**(b) Conflating equity percentage with control.** 78% is far above every meaningful threshold (50% ordinary, 75% special resolution in most jurisdictions). The real control question is board composition, reserved matters/protective provisions, drag-along, information rights, and forced-exit timing. A minority round taking founders to, say, 62% may cost less control than a covenant-heavy bank facility that hands a credit committee an effective veto over capex, hiring and acquisitions. The paper should state a **control floor as a rule** — e.g., never below 55% economic, never cede board majority, never accept investor veto over pricing, hiring or capacity decisions — and then test every instrument against that floor. That reframing (debt can cost more control than equity) is the single most valuable insight available here, and its absence would be a substantive failure, not a stylistic one.

**(c) Accepting "demand exceeds capacity" and "the window is closing" as facts.** Both are load-bearing and both are unverified.
- Demand > capacity at current prices means **price is below clearing**. A price increase is the cheapest capital in the structure: it funds capacity, rations demand toward better customers, and is non-dilutive and covenant-free. Any draft that omits pricing from the financing options has skipped the first option.
- The rival's raise is not automatically a threat. A capital-subsidised competitor may destroy segment economics rather than capture the segment. The window's real half-life depends on switching costs, contract length, installed base, IP, regulatory or distribution lock-in — not on the rival's press release. The paper must estimate window duration explicitly and note that the whole recommendation is contingent on it.

**(d) Ignoring the *shape* of the capital need.** "Capacity, hiring, and market expansion" are three different assets with three different correct funding sources: capex is asset-backed and debt-financeable; working capital is revolver/receivables-financeable; hiring and market entry are unsecured, high-failure-rate spend that should be funded by equity or retained cash. A single blended raise for all three is a common and expensive error. Match funding to asset life and recoverability.

**(e) Presenting a strawman "organic growth" option.** The disciplined-organic case must be argued at full strength or the comparison is rigged: contract manufacturing/outsourced capacity instead of owned capex, customer prepayments and deposits, extended supplier terms, deliberate segment and geography narrowing, higher prices, deferred hiring in non-bottleneck functions, ESOP in lieu of cash comp. Quantify what growth rate that actually sustains (a company doubling every two years and generating cash may fund more than the framing implies).

**(f) Omitting the downside scenario.** Covenant-heavy debt is only dangerous conditional on a growth stall. The paper needs a stress case — growth halves, gross margin compresses two points — and must show covenant headroom, cure rights, cross-default and personal-guarantee exposure under it. Equity's cost is dilution; debt's cost is *loss of the company* in a tail case. That asymmetry must be priced, not mentioned.

## 4. Missing quantitative spine

The request supplies no numbers. The draft therefore must **declare** a baseline rather than write around it. The prior work's tagging convention (`[V]` verifiable / `[R]` researchable / `[D]` design target) is genuinely useful here and should be carried over, because this paper mixes term-sheet market norms (`[R]`), tax/security law (`[V]`), and chosen dilution and leverage limits (`[D]`).

Minimum quantities needed for the argument to be checkable:
- Revenue, EBITDA margin, cash conversion, current net cash/debt.
- Capacity gap in units and the capex per unit of added capacity.
- Total funding requirement split across capex / working capital / opex-expansion, by year.
- Incremental ROIC on capacity spend — this is the number that decides whether debt is safe.
- Dilution arithmetic at two or three valuation points, and the implied founder stake.
- Blended cost of capital per structure, including warrant and ratchet cost.

## 5. Structural recommendations for the redraft

- **Lead with the recommendation in one paragraph**, as the prior paper does — a specific stack (e.g., asset-backed facility for capex + revolver for working capital + a tranched minority round staged against milestones, with a pre-agreed valuation step-up on the second tranche), not a discussion.
- **One comparison table** on the three named criteria plus cost of capital, downside severity, and speed-to-cash. Keep it to one table; the temptation is three.
- **Sequence and reversibility.** Cheapest and most reversible first: pricing, then working-capital debt, then asset-backed capex debt, then equity for the irrecoverable spend. Note which steps are one-way doors.
- **Staging gates with named owners and dates**, and — borrowing the prior paper's best device — an explicit statement of *what result would flip the recommendation*. Pre-committing the falsifier is what makes staging real rather than decorative.
- **Walk-away conditions as red lines**, one set per source, expressed as thresholds a lawyer or CFO could test against a term sheet.
- Address **strategic/customer capital** and **secondary vs. primary** (partial founder liquidity can reduce risk-aversion and make a lower headline valuation tolerable) — both are commonly omitted.
- State the **cost to the core** of each option, per the prior document's §0.3 rule. It transfers directly: management attention consumed by a diligence process, covenant reporting overhead, board-meeting load.

## 6. Length and tone

# Critic Review — "Growth-Financing Strategy" request

## 1. Blocking finding: there is no output to review

The `[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]` block is empty. Nothing was produced against the new request. This is a hard fail regardless of any other consideration, and it cannot be scored on quality, only on absence.

The only substantive content in the packet is the *prior* deliverable — a v2.0 board paper on international demand/supply entry for a €78m apparel brand. That artefact answers a different question for what appears to be a different company (no mention of 78% founder equity, doubling revenue, capacity constraints, or a funded rival). A redraft must not silently inherit its facts.

Because there is nothing to critique line-by-line, the remainder of this review functions as a specification the next draft will be judged against, plus the failure modes most likely to appear in a first attempt.

## 2. What the request actually demands (a completeness checklist)

The prompt contains five explicit deliverables. A draft missing any one of them is incomplete:

1. **A recommended growth-financing strategy** (a single position, not a menu).
2. **A four-way comparison** — debt / minority equity / hybrid instruments / disciplined organic growth — **evaluated against three named criteria**: risk tolerance, competitive window, founders' control preferences. This is a 4×3 grid at minimum; prose that discusses each option in isolation without cross-comparison on the same axes does not satisfy it.
3. **A proposed funding structure** — instruments, amounts, order of drawdown, sources.
4. **Staging milestones** — what unlocks each tranche.
5. **Walk-away conditions for each source** — five sets (including organic), pre-committed and testable.

Two of these (4 and 5) are where generic strategy writing usually collapses into platitude. "Revisit if performance deteriorates" is not a walk-away condition. "Decline any term sheet with a >1x participating preference, a redemption right inside 7 years, or investor consent over hiring/budget below €Xm" is.

## 3. Errors of framing the redraft is likely to make

**(a) Treating this as a valuation dispute when it is a structure dispute.** The founders think the growth fund's price is low. The paper must test whether *price* or *terms* is the binding constraint. A "low" headline valuation with a clean 1x non-participating preference, no ratchet, and a founder-majority board may be cheaper than a high headline number carrying a 2x participating preference and a redemption put. Any draft that argues about pre-money multiples without decomposing structural cost has missed the actual decision.

**(b) Conflating equity percentage with control.** 78% is far above every meaningful threshold (50% ordinary, 75% special resolution in most jurisdictions). The real control question is board composition, reserved matters/protective provisions, drag-along, information rights, and forced-exit timing. A minority round taking founders to, say, 62% may cost less control than a covenant-heavy bank facility that hands a credit committee an effective veto over capex, hiring and acquisitions. The paper should state a **control floor as a rule** — e.g., never below 55% economic, never cede board majority, never accept investor veto over pricing, hiring or capacity decisions — and then test every instrument against that floor. That reframing (debt can cost more control than equity) is the single most valuable insight available here, and its absence would be a substantive failure, not a stylistic one.

**(c) Accepting "demand exceeds capacity" and "the window is closing" as facts.** Both are load-bearing and both are unverified.
- Demand > capacity at current prices means **price is below clearing**. A price increase is the cheapest capital in the structure: it funds capacity, rations demand toward better customers, and is non-dilutive and covenant-free. Any draft that omits pricing from the financing options has skipped the first option.
- The rival's raise is not automatically a threat. A capital-subsidised competitor may destroy segment economics rather than capture the segment. The window's real half-life depends on switching costs, contract length, installed base, IP, regulatory or distribution lock-in — not on the rival's press release. The paper must estimate window duration explicitly and note that the whole recommendation is contingent on it.

**(d) Ignoring the *shape* of the capital need.** "Capacity, hiring, and market expansion" are three different assets with three different correct funding sources: capex is asset-backed and debt-financeable; working capital is revolver/receivables-financeable; hiring and market entry are unsecured, high-failure-rate spend that should be funded by equity or retained cash. A single blended raise for all three is a common and expensive error. Match funding to asset life and recoverability.

**(e) Presenting a strawman "organic growth" option.** The disciplined-organic case must be argued at full strength or the comparison is rigged: contract manufacturing/outsourced capacity instead of owned capex, customer prepayments and deposits, extended supplier terms, deliberate segment and geography narrowing, higher prices, deferred hiring in non-bottleneck functions, ESOP in lieu of cash comp. Quantify what growth rate that actually sustains (a company doubling every two years and generating cash may fund more than the framing implies).

**(f) Omitting the downside scenario.** Covenant-heavy debt is only dangerous conditional on a growth stall. The paper needs a stress case — growth halves, gross margin compresses two points — and must show covenant headroom, cure rights, cross-default and personal-guarantee exposure under it. Equity's cost is dilution; debt's cost is *loss of the company* in a tail case. That asymmetry must be priced, not mentioned.

## 4. Missing quantitative spine

The request supplies no numbers. The draft therefore must **declare** a baseline rather than write around it. The prior work's tagging convention (`[V]` verifiable / `[R]` researchable / `[D]` design target) is genuinely useful here and should be carried over, because this paper mixes term-sheet market norms (`[R]`), tax/security law (`[V]`), and chosen dilution and leverage limits (`[D]`).

Minimum quantities needed for the argument to be checkable:
- Revenue, EBITDA margin, cash conversion, current net cash/debt.
- Capacity gap in units and the capex per unit of added capacity.
- Total funding requirement split across capex / working capital / opex-expansion, by year.
- Incremental ROIC on capacity spend — this is the number that decides whether debt is safe.
- Dilution arithmetic at two or three valuation points, and the implied founder stake.
- Blended cost of capital per structure, including warrant and ratchet cost.

## 5. Structural recommendations for the redraft

- **Lead with the recommendation in one paragraph**, as the prior paper does — a specific stack (e.g., asset-backed facility for capex + revolver for working capital + a tranched minority round staged against milestones, with a pre-agreed valuation step-up on the second tranche), not a discussion.
- **One comparison table** on the three named criteria plus cost of capital, downside severity, and speed-to-cash. Keep it to one table; the temptation is three.
- **Sequence and reversibility.** Cheapest and most reversible first: pricing, then working-capital debt, then asset-backed capex debt, then equity for the irrecoverable spend. Note which steps are one-way doors.
- **Staging gates with named owners and dates**, and — borrowing the prior paper's best device — an explicit statement of *what result would flip the recommendation*. Pre-committing the falsifier is what makes staging real rather than decorative.
- **Walk-away conditions as red lines**, one set per source, expressed as thresholds a lawyer or CFO could test against a term sheet.
- Address **strategic/customer capital** and **secondary vs. primary** (partial founder liquidity can reduce risk-aversion and make a lower headline valuation tolerable) — both are commonly omitted.
- State the **cost to the core** of each option, per the prior document's §0.3 rule. It transfers directly: management attention consumed by a diligence process, covenant reporting overhead, board-meeting load.

## 6. Length and tone

The prior artefact's register — board paper, decision sought stated up front, uncertainty tagged, contingencies pre-committed — is the right target. Aim for a tight, fully-specified paper rather than a long one; every section should either move the decision or be cut. Avoid the prior draft's occasional over-assertion (e.g., unqualified claims about permanent competitor advantage); in a financing paper the equivalent trap is asserting market norms for terms as if they were verified facts.

---

# HOW WE FUND THE NEXT DOUBLING
## A staged capital stack: price first, secured debt second, minority equity only for the money we cannot get back

**Board decision paper | v1.0**
*(Term-sheet drafts, lender term-sheet comparisons and the Gate 0 research brief sit in Annex 1–3 and are not required for this decision.)*

No instrument is signed and no valuation is accepted at this meeting. The equity price decision becomes irrevocable only at Gate 3.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

We are not short of capital in aggregate; we are short of it for about **[20] months**. Base-case cumulative funding gap peaks at €[20]m in month [22] and self-liquidates from FY3 as the capacity we are buying converts to cash — so the correct answer is a **timing structure, not a single raise** (§3.3). We recommend, in this order: **(1) a realised price increase of [4]%** on the constrained order book, which is the cheapest capital available to us — non-dilutive, covenant-free, immediately effective, and it rations scarce capacity toward better customers (§4.1); **(2) customer deposits and capacity-reservation prepayments** of €[4]m against long-lead orders; **(3) a €[10]m borrowing-base revolver** secured on receivables and inventory only, funding working-capital build; **(4) €[14]m of equipment finance** secured on the machines it buys, no all-asset debenture and no personal guarantees; and **(5) €[14]m of minority primary equity in two tranches (€8m + €6m)**, the second at a pre-agreed step-up, used **only** for the irrecoverable spend — hiring, market entry, brand, systems — because that spend has no collateral value and must not be financed with instruments that can foreclose. We reject the framing that this is a valuation dispute: on the arithmetic in §4.4, the difference between the fund's €[110]m and the founders' €[150]m is worth ~[2] points of founder ownership, while a single bad structural term (2× participating preference plus accruing dividend) is worth ~[19]m of founder proceeds at a €[200]m exit. **Price is the small variable; terms are the large one.** We also reject the assumption that debt protects control: a maintenance-covenant bank facility hands a credit committee an effective veto over capex, hiring and acquisitions, and in the stress case in §9 it is the only instrument in this paper that can cost us the company. Two claims here are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that demand genuinely exceeds capacity at a *higher* price, and that the competitive window is [18–30] months rather than [6]. Gate 0 tests exactly those two, and §7.4 states in advance what result flips the recommendation.

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |

### 0.3 In scope / out of scope

| Funding the capacity, hiring and market-entry plan to FY3 | Sale of the company; majority recapitalisation |

### 0.4 The rule of this document

**Every financing option carries a stated cost to the core business**, not only a cost of capital. Diligence consumes the CEO and CFO; covenants consume the finance function monthly; investor boards consume preparation days. These are quantified in §10 and are part of the comparison in §3.5, not a footnote to it.

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Debt or equity? | Which *slice* of the requirement are we funding — recoverable assets, self-liquidating working capital, or unrecoverable expansion opex — and what is the correct instrument for that slice? (§3.3) |

| How do we keep control? | Control is board seats, reserved matters and forced-exit rights, not percentage. Which instrument gives away the most *decision rights* per euro raised? (§2) |

## §2 The control floor (a rule, not a preference)

Founders hold [78]%, comfortably above the [50]% ordinary-resolution and [75]% special-resolution thresholds **[V — confirm for our jurisdiction]**. | # | Floor | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Founder economic ownership | never below **[55]%** pre-exit **[D]** |
